title: Chinese Hackberry: The Enoki Trees of Japan's Shrines and Roadsides
meta_description: Japan calls it enoki, once planted at every ri-marker on the Tokugawa highways. Three mapped: a Kyoto palace gate, a Kyoto shrine, a Hiroshima shrine.
intro: In Japan this tree is enoki, and for two and a half centuries it did a job before it did anything ornamental: the Tokugawa shogunate planted one, or a red pine, at every ichirizuka, the paired earthen mounds that marked each ri of the great highways out of Edo, so a traveller had shade to rest in as well as a distance to measure. Most of those mounds are gone; a few survive as protected sites with the tree still standing on them. Shrines took to the species for the same reason city wards do now: it grows fast, broad and long-lived, wide enough in the crown to be worth wrapping in a sacred rope when a shrine decides a tree has become its shintai. All three mapped so far are measured rather than dated, because Japan's local surveys record girth, height and crown spread as a 'pride tree' or giant-tree designation and leave age to whoever asks later: a Kyoto Imperial Palace gate hackberry with a canopy nearly ten metres wider than the tree is tall, a Nashinoki Shrine hackberry logged at 21 metres, and a Hiroshima shrine hackberry that quietly out-girths the celebrated camphor sharing its grounds. Three are mapped, in two cities.
